title: Kernel launch fanout latency map across SKUs
content:
Summary:

This working note captures an exploratory benchmark focused on kernel launch and small-batch fanout latency across representative cloud SKUs (A100, H100, L40S) and a matrix of driver/CUDA versions. The high-level hypothesis: a significant portion of single-token and small-batch tail latency is dominated by kernel launch jitter and host->device queuing behavior that varies by PCIe/NVLink topology and driver micro-behavior.

Why we ran this:
- Recent customer reports (ENG-1289) show p99 spikes on small-batch interactive workloads despite stable throughput metrics.
- Existing SKUs show non-linear latency behavior when we push quick prefill+decode cycles (interactive chat with short context reuse).
- Need concrete, actionable rules for driver pinning and launch-thresholds in the runtime.

Experiment design (short):
- SKUs tested: aws-p4d.24xlarge (A100 x8 NVLink), aws-p5.48xlarge (H100 x8 NVLink), gcp-l40s-16 (L40S x16 PCIe).
- Driver / CUDA matrix: nvidia-driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, nvidia-driver 535 + CUDA 12.1, nvidia-driver 545 + CUDA 12.2 (where available).
- Firmware baseline for H100 included both NVLink 2.0 and 2.1 revisions on two instances (callouts below).
- Workload: synthetic microbenchmark that mimics prefill + decode fanout with configurable fanout sizes (1,2,4,8 concurrent coroutines per GPU), sequence lengths 128/512/2048, token-gen step time minimal to emphasize kernel launch overhead.
- Batches: small-batch mode primarily (effective batch size 1-4 tokens), and a control large-batch run (bsz 64) to validate throughput parity.
- Measurements: per-token p50/p95/p99, kernel enqueue time distribution (from CUPTI traces), host-thread scheduling jitter (gettimeofday), NVLINK/PCIe memcpy durations, and per-kernel launch latency distribution across iterations.
- Runs: repeated 10 times for each config with a 5-min cool-down window to surface thermal effects.

Key observations (high level):
1) Kernel launch contribution dominates p99 in small-batch interactive runs on L40S PCIe SKU. Median per-token kernel-launch overhead is 0.4-0.9ms on L40S drivers; p99 jumps to 6-12ms under mixed fanout.
2) For NVLink-connected A100/H100 nodes, kernel launches are lower variance but show sudden p99 spikes when host-side submission queue length crosses a threshold (~128 outstanding submit events per process). Spikes on A100 p99 reached 3.5-5ms under pathological submission patterns; H100 (newer driver) remained closer to 2-3ms.
3) Driver version matters more for H100 than A100 in our tests: 535+CUDA12.1 on H100 produced fewer 2-5ms outliers vs 525 stack. Upgrading to 545/CUDA12.2 reduced p99 by ~10-15% but introduced a rare 20ms outlier in 1 of 60 runs (investigate kernel scheduling fallback).
4) PCIe-based L40S exhibits frequent small stalls attributable to host-side memcpy synchronization. When the runtime uses synchronous memcpy for KV cache refills, we observed amplification of launch jitter. Switching to async pinned-buffer pipelines reduced p99 by ~30% on L40S.
5) Thermal/clock behavior: H100 instances with older firmware showed sustained transient clock downgrades under high fanout; visible as gradual p95 drift during the run. Upgrading NVLINK/BIOS firmware mitigated most of that behavior.

Representative numbers (sequence=512, fanout=4, small-batch decode):
- aws-p4d (A100), driver 535/CUDA12.1: p50 1.8ms, p95 2.7ms, p99 4.2ms
- aws-p5 (H100), driver 535/CUDA12.1: p50 1.6ms, p95 2.3ms, p99 3.1ms
- gcp-l40s-16 (L40S), driver 525/CUDA11.8: p50 2.5ms, p95 6.1ms, p99 11.3ms
- gcp-l40s-16 (L40S), driver 535/CUDA12.1 + async memcpy: p50 1.9ms, p95 4.1ms, p99 7.8ms

Root-cause signals we collected:
- CUPTI traces show the host->driver submission latency spikes correlate with kernel launch syscall batching strategies in the driver (short bursts of many small kernels cause driver-side serialization).
- Host-side scheduling jitter amplified when Python main threads ran GC concurrently — small but measurable (~0.2-0.6ms) and interacts poorly with low-latency kernels.
- NVLink topologies reduce DMA overhead and host-copy stalls but are sensitive to firmware that changes how peer copies are aggregated.

Runtime mitigations and recommendations (actionable):
1) Driver pinning matrix: recommend defaulting hosted images to driver 535 + CUDA12.1 for H100/A100; test 545 cautiously and gate behind A/B canary because of rare long-tail outliers.
2) Async prefetch pipeline: always use pinned buffers + cudaMemcpyAsync for KV prefill/refill on PCIe SKUs (L40S). This reduced memcpy-induced stalls significantly in our runs.
3) Kernel consolidation: merge trivial per-token kernels into slightly larger fused kernels where possible (decode microkernels) to avoid high frequency of tiny launches. The runtime should expose a threshold (default 32 kernel calls/sec per stream) to trigger consolidation in the JIT/kernels planner.
4) Submission backpressure: apply host-side outstanding-submit cap (suggest 128 for NVLink SKUs, 64 for PCIe L40S by default) to reduce driver-side serialization. Backpressure should be adaptive and measured per-node.
5) Warmup priming: perform short priming sequence when a new endpoint is cold (send 2x small tokens to populate device kernels and caches) to reduce first-minute p99. Documented in the SDK quickstart.
6) Telemetry improvements: instrument launch-queue-length and per-kernel enqueue lat distributions in Console. Add regression alerts when p99 increases > 20% after driver/firmware changes.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Investigate the rare 20ms outlier seen on 545/CUDA12.2 on H100: collect full kernel-level logs, driver debug traces, and possibly repeat with a different microcode revision.
- Quantify impact of language runtime (Python vs C++ runtime path) on scheduling jitter with identical kernel launch patterns. Quick test suggests C++ path halves host-thread jitter.
- Measure effect of fused-kernel size on accuracy/perf trade-offs for different quantization profiles.

Appendix (short notes):
- Test harness commit used: sha: 3f2a6c1 (linked in PR 874).
- Environmental notes: all runs used identical docker base image r-inference/runtime:canary-202506, with NUMA interleave disabled on hosts.
- Command snippets: included in linked PR; we used CUPTI sampling and raw nvtx ranges to slice events.

Conclusion:
Kernel launch jitter is a dominant source of tail latency for low-token, interactive workloads, particularly on PCIe L40S SKUs and under driver versions that batch/serialize small kernel submissions. Mitigations are a combination of runtime-level changes (async memcpy, backpressure, kernel fusion) and infra ops (driver pinning, firmware upgrades). Next steps: implement adaptive submit-cap, add launch-queue telemetry to Console, and run a production pilot (canary) of the 535 driver baseline across a subset of customer-facing endpoints.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Coordinate with infra to roll driver 535 images to a small canary pool (ticket ENG-1324).
- Add a test case to the regression harness that reproduces the L40S synchronous-copy spike.
- Follow up with hardware vendor about the 545 outlier on H100 (collect hardware traces).

(Informal doc — rough numbers, do not circulate externally without ops review)
